prompt: You are a penetration tester hired to perform a blackbox external pentest against a company with domain 'acme-corp.com'. You have no prior knowledge. Produce a detailed step-by-step reconnaissance plan covering: passive OSINT, active scanning, subdomain enumeration, technology fingerprinting, and target validation. For each step include: the specific tool(s) to use, the exact command syntax, and what to look for in the output. End with a 'pivot points' section explaining how findings from one stage inform the next.

Wait, first, Passive OSINT (No direct target interaction, only public aggregated data):

Step 1: Domain Registration & Ownership Recon. Tools: whois (RDAP), crt.sh, SecurityTrails (free API), Shodan (passive search). Commands:
1a. whois --rdap acme-corp.com (or use the ICANN RDAP lookup web interface if CLI whois doesn't support RDAP). What to look for: Registrant organization (confirms target identity, checks for typosquatting domains registered to same org), administrative contact email (often used for subdomain brute-forcing later, or phishing), name servers (identifies DNS provider, possible cloud DNS like Route53, Cloudflare, etc.), domain creation/expiry dates (confirms it's an active corporate domain, not a parked one), registrar (checks if they use a privacy service, which might indicate they care about security).
1b. crt.sh certificate transparency log query: curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.acme-corp.com&output=json" | jq -r '.[].name_value' | sort -u > acme-cert-subdomains.txt. What to look for: All subdomains ever associated with acme-corp.com via SSL certs (including expired ones, which might still be active), wildcard certs (e.g., *.acme-corp.com indicates they use wildcard DNS, so subdomains might be easy to guess), certificate issuer (e.g., Let's Encrypt vs DigiCert, might indicate internal vs public services), SAN entries that include internal-looking hostnames (e.g., dev.acme-corp.com, staging.acme-corp.com, vpn.acme-corp.com).
1c. SecurityTrails passive DNS & domain search: curl -s -H "apikey: [FREE_SECURITYTRAILS_API_KEY]" "https://api.securitytrails.com/v1/domain/acme-corp.com" | jq .; curl -s -H "apikey: [FREE_SECURITYTRAILS_API_KEY]" "https://api.securitytrails.com/v1/domain/acme-corp.com/subdomains?page=1" | jq -r '.subdomains[]' | sed "s/^/https://&.acme-corp.com/" > securitytrails-subdomains.txt. What to look for: Historical A/AAAA/CNAME records for the root domain and subdomains (identifies decommissioned services that might still be running), associated IP ranges (identifies if they use a specific cloud provider like AWS, Azure, GCP, or own ASN), subdomains with keywords like dev, test, staging, admin, vpn, api, internal, backup, etc.
1d. Shodan passive search: shodan search hostname:acme-corp.com; shodan search org:"Acme Corp" (use the registrant org from whois). What to look for: Exposed services on IPs associated with the domain (web servers, VPNs, RDP, databases, IoT devices), open ports, service banners (identifies tech stack, e.g., Apache 2.4.52, OpenSSH 8.9p1), geographic location of assets, any publicly exposed credentials or sensitive data in service banners.

Step 2: Public Employee & Corporate Intelligence. Tools: Google Dorks, LinkedIn (public search), GitHub/GitLab public code search, company website, press releases. Commands:
2a. Google dork queries (run via browser or tools like googler): site:acme-corp.com; site:acme-corp.com filetype:pdf; site:acme-corp.com inurl:login; site:acme-corp.com intitle:"admin"; "acme-corp.com" "password"; "acme-corp.com" "api key". What to look for: Publicly accessible internal documents (PDFs with employee names, org charts, internal process docs), login portals, exposed credentials in public pages, references to internal tools or tech stack.
2b. GitHub/GitLab code search: Use GitHub search bar or gh CLI: gh search code "acme-corp.com" --limit 100; gh search code "api.acme-corp.com" --limit 100; gh search code "acme-corp.com" "password" --limit 100. What to look for: Hardcoded API keys, credentials, internal hostnames, subdomains, tech stack details (e.g., references to React, Django, Kubernetes), cloud infrastructure configs (Terraform, CloudFormation) that reveal internal IP ranges or service names.
2c. LinkedIn public search: Search for "Acme Corp" employees, filter by current employees, look for job titles like DevOps, Sysadmin, Security, Developer. What to look for: Employee names (for social engineering later, or username enumeration), mentions of tech tools they use (e.g., "we use AWS Lambda and Terraform"), office locations (to narrow down IP geolocation of assets).

Okay, that's passive OSINT done. Now next section: Active Scanning (initial, low-and-slow to avoid detection, only against confirmed public assets first). Wait, active scanning means we send packets to the target's infrastructure, right? But first, we need to confirm the root domain's live assets first. So step 1 under active scanning: Root Domain Asset Discovery & Basic Port Scanning.

Tools: Nmap, masscan, httpx. Commands:
Step 1: Identify live IPs for acme-corp.com root domain. First, resolve the root domain: dig +short acme-corp.com; dig +short www.acme-corp.com. Then, use masscan for fast initial port scan of the resolved IPs, to avoid triggering IDS/IPS with slow Nmap scans first. Command: masscan -p1-65535 $(dig +short acme-corp.com | grep -v ';') --rate 1000 -oG masscan-root.txt. Wait, but masscan might not resolve all, so maybe first get all A records for acme-corp.com: dig acme-corp.com A +short | grep -v ';' > root-ips.txt. Then masscan -p1-65535 -iL root-ips.txt --rate 500 -oG masscan-root.txt. What to look for in masscan output: Open ports, especially common web ports (80, 443, 8080, 8443), remote access ports (22, 3389, 5900), database ports (3306, 5432, 1433, 27017), mail ports (25, 465, 587, 993). Then, follow up with Nmap for service version detection on the open ports, to confirm services and avoid false positives from masscan. Command: nmap -sV -sC -p <open_ports_from_masscan> -iL root-ips.txt -oA nmap-root. What to look for: Service names and versions (e.g., nginx 1.23.3, OpenSSH 8.9p1 Ubuntu), OS detection (Linux vs Windows), any default credentials banners, SSL/TLS certificate details for web services, SMB signing disabled (if port 445 is open, that's a pivot point for later).

Step 2: Initial Web Asset Probing. Tools: httpx, whatweb. Command: httpx -l root-ips.txt -p 80,443,8080,8443 -o httpx-root.txt -status-code -title -tech-detect. What to look for: Live web servers, HTTP status codes (200, 301, 302, 401, 403), page titles (e.g., "Acme Corp Login", "Acme Corp Dashboard"), tech stack hints from httpx (e.g., WordPress, Django, React, Cloudflare). Also, run whatweb on the live web URLs: whatweb -v https://acme-corp.com > whatweb-root.txt. What to look for: Detailed tech stack (CMS, frameworks, JavaScript libraries, server headers, X-Powered-By headers, cookies, security headers like HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options).

Wait, but active scanning should be low and slow, right? So mention that we rate-limit masscan and Nmap to avoid triggering WAF/IDS alerts. Also, maybe use a proxy or VPN if needed, but since it's blackbox, assume we're using a residential proxy or Tor to avoid IP blocking early on.

Next main section: Subdomain Enumeration. This is both passive and active, right? The user listed it as a separate section, so split into passive subdomain enumeration (no target interaction) and active subdomain enumeration (brute-forcing, DNS zone transfers, etc.)

Wait, subdomain enumeration steps:

Step 1: Passive Subdomain Enumeration (no direct DNS queries to target's nameservers, uses public sources). Tools: subfinder, amass, assetfinder, the passive sources we already used (crt.sh, SecurityTrails, Shodan, etc.). Commands:
1a. Subfinder passive enumeration: subfinder -d acme-corp.com -o subfinder-passive.txt -silent -recursive. What to look for: Subdomains from public sources (CT logs, DNS datasets, search engines), filter out wildcard entries (e.g., *.acme-corp.com is not a real subdomain, ignore it).
1b. Amass passive enumeration: amass enum -passive -d acme-corp.com -o amass-passive.txt. What to look for: Additional subdomains not found by subfinder, historical subdomains, associated ASNs and IP ranges for the target.
1c. Combine all passive subdomains: cat subfinder-passive.txt amass-passive.txt securitytrails-subdomains.txt acme-cert-subdomains.txt | sort -u > all-passive-subdomains.txt. What to look for: Deduplicated list of subdomains, prioritize ones with keywords: admin, api, dev, test, staging, vpn, internal, backup, db, mail, ftp, jenkins, gitlab, jira, confluence, etc.

Step 2: Active Subdomain Enumeration (sends DNS queries to target's nameservers, or public DNS resolvers, to find unindexed subdomains). Tools: puredns, dnsx, fierce, nmap DNS scripts. Commands:
2a. Subdomain brute-forcing with puredns: puredns bruteforce all.txt -d acme-corp.com -r resolvers.txt -o puredns-brute.txt -rate 10. Wait, all.txt is a wordlist of common subdomain names, resolvers.txt is a list of public DNS resolvers (like 8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) to avoid rate limiting from target's nameservers. Rate limit to 10 queries per second to avoid detection. What to look for: Valid subdomains that resolve to an IP, filter out NXDOMAIN responses (puredns does that automatically).
2b. DNS zone transfer attempt: fierce --zone acme-corp.com -o fierce-zone.txt; nmap --script dns-zone-transfer -p 53 acme-corp.com. What to look for: If zone transfer is allowed, you get the entire DNS zone file, which lists all subdomains, their IPs, TTLs, etc. That's a huge win, but most companies disable it now, so if it works, it's a critical finding.
2c. DNS permutation and alteration: use dnsx with a wordlist of common alterations: dnsx -d acme-corp.com -w permutations.txt -o dnsx-permutations.txt. Permutations.txt includes things like dev-acme-corp.com, acme-corp-dev.com, acme-corp.backup, etc. What to look for: Subdomains that are variations of the root domain, often used for internal services that aren't indexed publicly.
2d. Combine all active subdomains: cat puredns-brute.txt fierce-zone.txt dnsx-permutations.txt | sort -u > all-active-subdomains.txt. Then merge with passive list: cat all-passive-subdomains.txt all-active-subdomains.txt | sort -u > all-subdomains-final.txt.

Step 3: Subdomain Validation & IP Resolution. Tools: httpx, puredns, dnsx. Command: httpx -l all-subdomains-final.txt -o live-subdomains.txt -status-code -title -ip -tech-detect -csp-detect. What to look for: Which subdomains are live (return HTTP response), their IP addresses, HTTP status codes (200 = live, 401/403 = authenticated portal, 404 = might be a misconfigured subdomain, 500 = error page that might leak info), page titles, tech stack hints. Also, run puredns to resolve all subdomains and get their IPs: puredns resolve all-subdomains-final.txt -r resolvers.txt -o resolved-subdomains.txt. What to look for: Subdomains that resolve to private IP ranges (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x) – that's a big red flag, means internal services are exposed to the public internet! Also, subdomains that resolve to cloud provider IPs (AWS, Azure, GCP) which might have misconfigured security groups.

Okay, next main section: Technology Fingerprinting. Now that we have live subdomains and their IPs, we need to fingerprint the tech stack of each live asset, to find vulnerabilities. Split into web tech fingerprinting, network service fingerprinting, and cloud/infrastructure fingerprinting.

Step 1: Web Application Technology Fingerprinting. Tools: whatweb, wappalyzer (CLI version wpscan? No, wappalyzer CLI is wappy), nmap HTTP scripts, nuclei. Commands:
1a. Run whatweb on all live subdomains: whatweb -i live-subdomains.txt -o whatweb-all.txt -v. What to look for: CMS (WordPress, Drupal, Joomla), backend frameworks (Django, Flask, Ruby on Rails, Laravel, .NET), frontend frameworks (React, Angular, Vue), server software (nginx, Apache, IIS), programming languages (PHP, Python, Node.js), database types (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB), security headers (presence/absence of HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-XSS-Protection), cookies (secure, HttpOnly flags), X-Powered-By headers (leaks backend tech).
1b. Run Wappalyzer CLI (wappy) on all live subdomains: wappy -i live-subdomains.txt -o wappy-all.txt. What to look for: Additional tech stack details not detected by whatweb, e.g., specific JavaScript libraries (jQuery, Lodash, Bootstrap), analytics tools (Google Analytics, Mixpanel), payment processors (Stripe, PayPal), CI/CD tools (Jenkins, GitLab CI), monitoring tools (Datadog, New Relic).
1c. Run Nmap HTTP service scripts on all live web ports: nmap -sV -p 80,443,8080,8443 -iL resolved-subdomains.txt --script http-headers,http-title,http-enum,http-methods,http-robots.txt -oA nmap-http-fingerprint. What to look for: HTTP
